• Common names: MTS, Red rim melania, Pest snail
  • Minimum tank size: does not matter
  • Breeding: very easy
  • Temperature tolerance: 11 to 32 °C; optimal 22–25 °C
  • Optimal KH: 1–12 (tolerates 0–25)
  • TDS (optimal): 100–300
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore / algae eater
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: creamy to brownish

Malaysian Trumpet Snails (Melanoides tuberculata) can be a desirable addition, especially to planted tanks, because they are great scavengers and help to control algae. However, they can also quickly become a nightmare when they start reproducing out of control in the tank.

They are very tough and live in a wide range of water parameters. In aquariums they are often considered pest snails, and they are the centre of many discussions in the hobby: some aquarists try to remove them as soon as possible, while others consider them useful and beneficial.

They usually arrive with plants through commercial trade. They can certainly get out of control, so that the tank becomes crowded with these snails.

The Malaysian Trumpet Snail is a freshwater gastropod native to Africa and Asia, and is now distributed worldwide, mainly thanks to its high adaptability to new environments. Today the species is established or reported in almost all regions between northern Argentina and Florida, USA, including the West Indies, as well as Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Paraguay.

According to some reports, it was probably introduced to North America (California and Florida) by the aquarium industry in the 1930s. By the mid-1960s M. tuberculata was reported from Texas, Arizona and the northern part of the Great Basin in southeastern Oregon. In the mid-1990s scientists reported it in springs of the Nevada portion of the Great Basin. It has continued to expand its range through most warm regions of the United States.

The snails are also found in northern Australia, in European Mediterranean countries and in hot springs in Austria, Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary.

NEVER release Malaysian Trumpet Snails into the wild. Melanoides tuberculata is one of the most invasive water snails in the world. It has been introduced to parts of Europe, South America, Central America and the southern United States, where it competes with native mollusks.

Malaysian Trumpet Snails occupy a variety of habitats, from weakly saline water close to sea level to freshwater at higher altitudes. The species thrives in a wide range of pH and hardness and is found on different kinds of substrate, most commonly muddy to sandy substrate, at depths between 0.25 and 3.7 m.

In nature these snails are most often found in slow or stagnant water and thrive in areas impacted by humans. They colonise stable water bodies such as ponds, lakes, irrigation canals, ditches, municipal drains, rivers, dams, streams and levees, mostly with low flow rates.
Tank size does not matter. For deliberately breeding these snails in optimal conditions, a 20–40 litre tank is enough.

This is the easiest part: Malaysian Trumpet Snails are ultimate survivalists in freshwater tanks. In nature they have shown an impressive capacity to invade a range of tropical and subtropical aquatic ecosystems. In aquariums, once established, they are very hard to remove, which is why they are also reported in the literature as a nuisance species.

Superpowers

  • They do not require a lot of oxygen. They tolerate low levels of dissolved oxygen and are highly resistant to pollution.
  • They resist desiccation. According to some studies, Melanoides tuberculata withstands a lack of water for prolonged periods of drought (up to 26 months), sealing the trapdoor and waiting for better times.
  • They tolerate salinity. Some individuals survive extreme salinities up to 45‰ for a short time, and half of them survive 82‰ saltwater. The snails become motionless (sealing the trapdoor) at 30‰ or greater.
  • They tolerate relatively low temperatures: down to 11 °C for 15 days, at which only 50% of the snails died.
  • They can live without food for weeks.
  • They survive chemical treatments (undiluted household bleach) better than non-operculate pest snails such as bladder snails or pond snails.
  • They are undemanding about water hardness and pH. Unless pH stays below 6.0 for months, they do not mind.
  • They are indifferent to ammonia; aquarists often use them to cycle tanks.

To breed them on purpose in optimal conditions, use a 20–40 litre tank, pH 7.0–8.0, temperature 22–25 °C, KH 6–15 and GH 1–12, with a substrate (sand or soil) deep enough for them to burrow in, and a sponge filter.

Copper

Like all snails, they are sensitive to copper; this is their weak point. In an experiment, adult snails were exposed for 96 hours in the laboratory to a range of copper, cadmium, zinc, lead, nickel, iron, aluminium and manganese concentrations. Copper was the most toxic metal. The LC50 value (the lethal concentration that kills 50% of the population) for 96-hour exposure to copper was 0.14, and for 48-hour exposure 0.39.

Watch out for copper if you use tap water or fertilisers in the tank.

Optimal temperature 22–25 °C (tolerates 11–32 °C), pH 7.0–8.0 (tolerates 6.0–10.0), GH 6–15 (tolerates 0–25), KH 1–12 (tolerates 0–25), TDS 100–300, nitrate below 40 ppm.

Shell deterioration is a common symptom in snails kept in water lacking sufficient dissolved minerals, particularly calcium, to develop and repair their shells. Most snails need water of at least medium hardness and pH 7.0–8.0 for proper shell development. Calcium-rich food can be added if, for example, the snails are being bred to feed pufferfish or crayfish; otherwise it is not necessary.

For breeding them on purpose: a small tank, a sponge filter, and a sand or soil substrate deep enough for burrowing. Small snails can get into filter intakes; in a powerhead they can clog the filter and in rare cases have broken impellers.

Malaysian Trumpet Snails are generalist herbivores and detritivores. In aquariums they feed on algae, microalgae (diatoms), bacteria, dead and decaying organic matter (animal tissue, meat, insects, vegetables or plants), leftover fish or shrimp food (pellets, flakes, algae wafers, etc.), debris and waste.

You do not need to feed them at all. They are extremely efficient scavengers and cleaners, and act as an indicator of the food balance in the tank. If you have a snail infestation, look at the feeding and maintenance regime.

They are completely plant safe and do not eat healthy, living plants. People sometimes confuse grazing with eating: if you see them eating a seemingly healthy plant, it is already dying, even if that has not yet shown. They trim and remove dead or decaying vegetation, leaving plants looking tended.

These snails are primarily crepuscular or nocturnal. They spend most of the daylight hours buried in mud or sand, which prevents gas pockets building up that can be very dangerous to fish or shrimp. They may come out in the daytime to forage, but this does not happen often. They can pull deeply into the shell and seal themselves off from the environment, and can survive a long time sealed in their shells.

They are peaceful and can live in any community tank. They are excellent food for Assassin snails, crayfish, loaches, pufferfish, oscars and others. There are some reports that Asolene spixi snails can also feed on them if very hungry. They have a thick shell and can endure the nipping of small fish.

Unless you are a biologist, it can be very hard (impossible) to see sexual dimorphism. Males can be distinguished from females by the shape of the shell and their red gonad: male tissue appears dark wine-red, and female tissue significantly less red when viewed through the thinner portions of the adapical shell.

Malaysian Trumpet Snails are not hermaphrodites. The species is viviparous (live-bearing) with parthenogenetic and sexual reproduction:

  • Parthenogenetic (virgin birth): females give birth to more female clones without a male. A single female can establish a self-sustaining colony of one genotypic clone in a new environment in just a few months.
  • Sexual reproduction is very rare but exists. It has been found in populations where males reached up to 66%. Some populations consist only of females, with a few sterile males.

The species shows rapid growth and early maturation. Depending on diet and temperature, snails reach sexual maturity at a shell height of 7–11 mm (in about 3–5 months). At a shell length of 20 mm adults reach maximum reproductive capacity, after which fertility gradually decreases. Snails larger than 25 mm stop reproducing but can continue to grow.

The number of developing young in the brood pouch varies from 1 to 91, but large females can produce 200+ young. The egg measures 0.01 mm in diameter and is surrounded by an egg capsule 0.15 mm in diameter from which embryos hatch. Embryos develop in brood pouches and are released as juveniles with up to 5–6 shell whorls. Many embryos do not develop into functional animals but disintegrate and become part of the food ingested by the developing embryos; the developing young feed on other egg yolks and brood-pouch reserves.

Newborn snails measure 1.5 to 2.0 mm and grow about 2.5 mm per month. Fully developed juveniles hatch between nightfall and midnight, possibly due to a general increase in activity at this time. Biologists noticed that the brooding time and the size of newborn snails decreased as the number of snails in the aquarium increased.

Adults are relatively small mollusks, 2 to 4 cm in their native range. Growth is fastest in the first year of life, when they can reach 21.31 mm; between the first and second year growth slows to 8.87 mm, and in later years they grow less than 1 mm per year. They live about 2 to 3.5 years and mature sexually at about 4 months, depending on temperature and feeding.

The species shows a broad range of shell variation (more than 27 morphs). The shell is distinctly elongated and conical, usually with 6 to 12 whorls, pale or creamy to dark brown with numerous reddish-brown flames and spots, although darker varieties also occur. Most adult shells have prominent ridges. The head is flattened, with a pair of tentacles with eyes at their bases and the mouth at the front. There is an operculum (trapdoor) and papillae at the end of the mantle.

The snail acts as an intermediate host for parasites of humans and other vertebrates, such as the trematode Gastrodiscus aegyptiacus; human infection occurs by eating raw fish infected by the parasite. Parasites appear to have a sterilising effect on female snails. In some places its colonisation is seen as beneficial to public health, because it reduces other snails that are intermediate hosts of disease, such as the snail that transmits the blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni.

Pros

  • They do not eat plants.
  • Amazing scavengers and good algae eaters.
  • Burrowing loosens the gravel and sifts sand or soil.
  • Thick shell that endures nipping by small fish.
  • Good tank mates for shrimp tanks.
  • Extremely hardy.

Cons

  • Small snails can get into the filter intake and clog filters.
  • They reproduce extremely fast.
  • Because they stay buried in the daytime, you never know how many you have.
  • Extremely hardy, so they are not easy to remove.
